nameStory: Purple lovegrass gets its common name from the beautiful purplish tinge that develops in its delicate, cloud-like flower clusters, especially as they mature. The 'love' part of the name comes from the genus Eragrostis, which means 'love grass' in Greek - though botanists aren't entirely sure why early scientists chose this romantic moniker for these graceful grasses.
description: Purple lovegrass is a delicate annual grass that forms small tufts, typically growing 6 inches to 2 feet tall. Its most striking feature is its airy, open flower cluster that spreads like a miniature cloud above the thin leaves. The entire plant has a fine, wispy appearance, and despite being called 'purple' lovegrass, it often appears more greenish or tan with subtle purple hints in the flower heads.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny flowers arranged in an open, branching cluster that feels delicate and almost weightless when touched, with a subtle purplish cast that's most noticeable in good light

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms small, neat tufts rather than spreading widely, with multiple stems arising from the base like a tiny fountain

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, thread-like leaves that feel smooth and soft between your fingers, typically 2-4 inches long and much thinner than a pencil

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Extremely tiny seeds that easily shake loose from the flower head when mature, feeling like fine sand if rubbed between fingers

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Overall plant feels soft and pliable, never rough or scratchy like some grasses, with a delicate quality that makes it seem almost fragile

habitat: Look for purple lovegrass in disturbed soils, roadsides, vacant lots, and other open, sunny areas throughout New England. It thrives in poor soils and seems to particularly enjoy sandy or gravelly ground where other plants struggle. You'll often find it growing alongside other weedy grasses and wildflowers in areas that have been recently disturbed by human activity.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as tiny tufts of thread-like green leaves, easily overlooked among other spring vegetation.
seasonality.summer: Flower clusters develop and become most visible, with the characteristic airy, open appearance that makes identification easiest.
seasonality.fall: Seeds mature and flower heads take on more pronounced purplish tones, then gradually turn tan as seeds disperse.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants die back completely, leaving no trace above ground until seeds germinate the following spring.

funFact: Purple lovegrass seeds are so tiny that a single plant can produce thousands of them, and they're light enough to travel for miles on the wind - which explains how this grass can suddenly appear in newly disturbed soil seemingly out of nowhere, like nature's own pioneer squad.
confusionNotes: Purple lovegrass is most easily confused with other small lovegrasses, especially tiny lovegrass, but purple lovegrass forms neater, more compact tufts rather than sprawling loosely. Remember: purple lovegrass stays 'put together' in tidy clumps, while tiny lovegrass tends to look more scattered and messy.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'Carolina lovegrass' in some regions, this species actually ranges from Canada all the way to Argentina, making it one of the most widely distributed grasses in the Americas. The name can be misleading since it's not particularly associated with the Carolinas.
compareHints: Among New England's lovegrasses, purple lovegrass is distinguished by its compact, tufted growth habit and relatively small size. Purple lovegrass (Eragrostis spectabilis) is much larger and showier, while tiny lovegrass spreads more loosely rather than forming neat tufts. The open, airy flower cluster of purple lovegrass is more delicate-looking than the denser heads of little lovegrass.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Purple Lovegrass is the showiest of New England's lovegrasses, with much larger and more colorful flower clusters than its relatives like Little Lovegrass or Teal Lovegrass.

Teal lovegrass stands out from its lovegrass relatives primarily by its wetland habitat - while purple lovegrass, little lovegrass, and most others prefer dry, disturbed soils, teal lovegrass is the water-lover of the family.
African lovegrass differs from other New England lovegrasses by its distinctive weeping growth habit and blue-gray foliage color.
Among the lovegrasses in New England, Little Lovegrass is one of the smallest and most delicate-looking.
Among New England's love-grasses, Jersey Love-grass is the most delicate and airy-looking.
Tiny lovegrass lives up to its name by being much smaller and more delicate than its lovegrass relatives like purple lovegrass, which forms more substantial clumps.

Among the lovegrasses, Frank's Lovegrass sits in the middle size-wise—larger than Tiny Lovegrass with its hair-thin appearance, but smaller and less showy than Purple Lovegrass which often forms more substantial clumps.
